hpi_details: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with asymmetric arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she caught pink eye from her toddler grandchild and has another stubborn urinary tract infection.
concerns: She is worried the infection has spread into her joint and will prevent her from walking down the aisle at her daughter's wedding next month.
expectations: She hopes to walk away with a course of strong antibiotics to clear up the urinary infection and medicated drops for her eyes.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Reactive Arthritis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management includes excluding septic or gonococcal arthritis, testing for an active triggering infection, and using clinician-directed symptom treatment; antibiotics treat an identified active infection, not the sterile arthritis itself.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: asymmetric arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis

Key HPI features: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with asymmetric arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Reactive Arthritis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Reactive Arthritis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Septic arthritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with joint swelling — must exclude septic/gonococcal arthritis.
management_principles: Exclude septic and disseminated gonococcal arthritis urgently when indicated; test and treat an identified active sexually transmitted or enteric infection according to local guidance, including partner management where appropriate
Use NSAIDs only after reviewing renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, anticoagulation, and pregnancy risks; refer for persistent or severe disease
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Clinical Guidance

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of asymmetric arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis. HPI: post-chlamydia or gastrointestinal infection.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Reactive Arthritis.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Reactive Arthritis.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Reactive Arthritis: NSAIDs, treat underlying infection if active, reassure. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Reactive Arthritis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Reactive Arthritis
Implement evidence-based management plan: NSAIDs, treat underlying infection if active, reassure

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune arthritis triggered by a preceding infection (often chlamydia or a GI infection), classically causing the triad of asymmetric arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis.
red_flags: Fever with joint swelling — must exclude septic/gonococcal arthritis

must_ask.say: Did you have a bladder/genital infection or diarrhea a few weeks before this started?
Which joints are affected, and is it the same on both sides?
Have your eyes been red or irritated?
Any burning with urination or discharge?
Can you tell me about your recent sexual activity?

history.answer: My right knee and left ankle have become swollen and painful, and my eyes have been red and burning for the past few days.
It's my right knee and my left ankle that are hurting, so it's just on one side for each joint, not matching.
It started about a week ago in my right knee, and then a few days later my left ankle flared up as well.
It's a constant, deep aching and throbbing pain, and at its worst it gets to about a 6 out of 10.
Both my right knee and left ankle are definitely swollen, feel warm to the touch, and look a bit pink.
They feel very stiff when I get out of bed in the morning, and it usually takes about an hour before they loosen up.
Walking, going down the hallway, or standing for too long makes the pain worse, while resting with my feet up helps ease it.
I can still put some weight on my feet, but I'm limping and climbing stairs is really difficult.
No, I haven't had any high fevers or shaking chills at all.
No, I haven't fallen, twisted either joint, heard any popping noises, or had my knee lock up on me.
No, I have never had painful or swollen joints like this in my life.
I've been feeling unusually tired and wiped out lately, but my weight has been completely steady.
Both of my eyes are red, burning, and watering, almost like I have pinkeye.
No, I don't have any rashes on my face or body, no dry mouth, and no sores inside my mouth.
The back of my left heel has been tender and sore to touch, but I don't have severe lower back stiffness or swollen sausage fingers.
Over the past week, I've had some burning when I urinate and I feel like I have to go more often, with a bit of thin discharge.
About three weeks ago, I had mild diarrhea and stomach cramps for two days after eating out, and no recent sore throat.
I haven't eaten a lot of red meat or seafood, I rarely drink, and I don't take any water pills.
No, I've never taken steroids or immune-suppressing drugs, and I've never had injections or surgery on my joints.
I am divorced and had a new sexual partner about four weeks ago without using a condom.
I've had no chronic health problems; I've always been very healthy.
I've never had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, just some over-the-counter ibuprofen over the past few days.
I don't have any known allergies to medications or anything else.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only have an occasional glass of wine socially, maybe once or twice a month.
I work in an office as an administrator, and I live with my adult daughter.
Nobody in my family has rheumatoid arthritis, gout, psoriasis, or any autoimmune conditions.
I went through menopause about five years ago, so my periods stopped completely and there's no possibility of pregnancy.
I assumed I picked up pink eye from my toddler granddaughter and that the burning when I pee is just another stubborn bladder infection.

I'm so worried this infection has gotten into my knee and will keep me from walking down the aisle at my daughter's wedding next month. I'm hoping you can prescribe a strong course of antibiotics for the infection and some drops to clear up my eyes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, pulse 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 37.1°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Alert and oriented female in mild discomfort, ambulating with a noticeable limp favoring the right leg.
Bilateral conjunctival injection and mild watery discharge present; sclerae non-icteric.
Oral mucous membranes are pink and moist without ulcerations; pharynx is non-erythematous.
Right knee and left ankle demonstrate moderate effusion, warmth, erythema, and tender range of motion, with focal tenderness at the left Achilles tendon insertion.
No psoriatic plaques, scalp scaling, fingernail pitting, or keratoderma blennorrhagica on the palms or soles.
External genitalia show mild erythema around the urethral meatus with scant clear mucoid discharge, but no vulvar ulcers or lesions.
No spinal process tenderness, normal lumbar spine motion, and negative bilateral straight-leg raise tests.
Antalgic gait with reluctance to bear full weight on the right knee and left ankle.
